This formula collection supports you during the Investment Finance lecture in the Bachelor of Business and Engineering program at THWS.

|--------------|-------------|

| $B$ | Budget (capital rationing) |

| $s$ | Tax rate |

| $TV_n$ | Terminal value of all inflows at $t = n$ (MIRR) |

| $Z_t$ | Interest payment in period $t$ |
| $\pi$ | Inflation rate |
| $\sigma$ | Standard deviation |

# Interest Calculation

## Fisher Equation

> **Symbol note:** In this section only, $r$ denotes the **real interest rate**. Elsewhere in this collection, $r$ is used for IRR and Yield to Maturity.

Approximate relationship between nominal rate, inflation, and real rate:

$$ r \approx i_{nom} - \pi $$

For high rates (above ~10 %), use the exact form:

$$ 1 + r = \frac{1 + i_{nom}}{1 + \pi} $$

## Simple Interest (without compounding)

$$ FV = PV \cdot (1 + n \cdot i) $$

## Compound Interest

$$ FV = PV \cdot (1 + i)^n $$

## Discounting

The inverse of compounding — transports a future value back to the present:

$$ PV = FV \cdot (1+i)^{-n} = \frac{FV}{(1+i)^n} $$

The factor $(1+i)^{-n}$ is the **Discount Factor** (Abzinsungsfaktor); it is always less than 1 for $i > 0$.

## Nominal vs. Effective Interest (Intra-year Compounding)

Relative interest rate for intra-year periods ($m$ = periods per year):

$$ i_{rel} = \frac{i_{nom}}{m} $$

### Simple Interest (Intra-year)

$n$ = complete years, $k$ = additional sub-annual periods:

$$ FV = PV \cdot \bigl(1 + (n \cdot m + k) \cdot i_{rel}\bigr) $$

### Compound Interest (Intra-year)

$$ FV = PV \cdot (1 + i_{rel})^{n \cdot m + k} $$

### Effective Annual Rate

The annual rate that yields the same result with one compounding per year:

$$ i_{eff} = \left(1 + \frac{i_{nom}}{m}\right)^m - 1 $$

> **Two meanings of "nominal":** $i_{nom}$ is nominal as opposed to *real* in the Fisher equation (before inflation) and as opposed to *effective* here (before intra-year compounding).

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Annuities & Perpetuities

## Ordinary Annuity (Nachschüssige Rente)

Present value of $n$ equal **end-of-period** payments of $C$:

$$ PV = C \cdot PVIFA(i,\,n) $$

Annual payment required to amortise or generate a lump sum $PV$:

$$ C = PV \cdot CRF(i,\,n) $$

Future value of $n$ equal end-of-period payments (savings plan):

$$ FV = C \cdot \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i} = C \cdot PVIFA(i,\,n) \cdot (1+i)^n $$

## Annuity Due (Vorschüssige Rente)

Payments occur at the **start** of each period (e.g. rent, leasing). Every payment is one period earlier, so the present value is higher by the factor $(1+i)$:

$$ PV_{\text{due}} = PV_{\text{ordinary}} \times (1+i) $$

## Present Value Interest Factor of an Annuity (PVIFA)

$$ PVIFA(i,\,n) = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i \cdot (1+i)^n} $$

## Capital Recovery Factor (CRF)

$$ CRF(i,\,n) = \frac{i \cdot (1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1} = \frac{1}{PVIFA(i,\,n)} $$

## Perpetuity

Present value of an infinite uniform payment stream:

$$ PV = \frac{C}{i} $$

## Growing Perpetuity

Present value of an infinite stream where payments grow at constant rate $g$ ($g < i$):

$$ PV = \frac{C_1}{i - g} $$

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Loan Amortization

## Debt Service

Every loan payment consists of an interest and a repayment component:

$$ K_t = Z_t + T_t \qquad \text{with } Z_t = R_{t-1} \cdot i $$

## Annuity Loan (Annuitätendarlehen)

Constant total payment per period (*Scissors Effect*: interest falls, repayment rises):

$$ K_t = C_0 \cdot CRF(i,\,n) = \text{constant} $$

## Constant Amortization Loan (Ratentilgungsdarlehen)

Equal principal repayment each period; total payment decreases linearly:

$$ T_t = \frac{C_0}{n} = \text{constant}, \qquad K_t = T_t + Z_t \quad \text{(declining)} $$

## Bullet Loan (Endfälliges Darlehen)

Interest-only payments throughout; full principal repaid at maturity:

$$ T_{1 \dots n-1} = 0, \qquad T_n = C_0, \qquad Z_t = C_0 \cdot i = \text{constant} $$

## Supplier Credit: Effective Interest Rate (Skonto)

$$ r_{\text{eff}} = \frac{s_k}{100 - s_k} \cdot \frac{360}{t_{\text{net}} - t_{\text{discount}}} \cdot 100 $$

where $s_k$ = cash discount percentage, $t_{\text{net}}$ = net payment term (days), $t_{\text{discount}}$ = early-payment term (days).

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Valuation

## Bond Valuation

A bond's price equals the present value of its coupon annuity plus the discounted par value ($C = F \cdot c$):

$$ P_0 = C \cdot PVIFA(r,\,n) + F \cdot (1+r)^{-n} $$

**Inverse problem — YTM from price (Linear Interpolation / Regula Falsi):**

Choose $r_1$ and $r_2$ such that they bracket the true YTM: one rate must give $P(r_1) > P_0$ (rate below YTM) and the other $P(r_2) < P_0$ (rate above YTM).

$$ r \approx r_1 + \frac{P(r_1) - P_0}{P(r_1) - P(r_2)} \cdot (r_2 - r_1) $$

## Preferred Stock (Perpetuity)

Fixed dividend $Div$ in perpetuity:

$$ P_0 = \frac{Div}{r} $$

## Common Stock — Dividend Discount Model (Gordon Growth Model)

Dividends growing at constant rate $g$ in perpetuity ($g < r$):

$$ P_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g} \qquad \text{with } D_1 = D_0 \cdot (1+g) $$

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Payback Period

Static payback: the year $T$ is the last full year in which the cumulative cash flows are still below $I_0$; the remainder is interpolated within year $T+1$:

$$ PP = T + \frac{I_0 - \sum_{t=1}^{T} CF_t}{CF_{T+1}} $$

The **discounted payback** $PP_{disc}$ uses the discounted cash flows $CF_t \cdot (1+i)^{-t}$ instead. Payback measures *how soon*, not *how much* — it ignores everything after the cut-off and is no substitute for the NPV.

# Net Present Value

$$ NPV = -I_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} CF_t \cdot (1+i)^{-t} + L_n \cdot (1+i)^{-n} $$

| $NPV$ | Decision |
|:-----:|:--------:|
| $> 0$ | **Accept** — project creates value above cost of capital |
| $= 0$ | Indifferent — project exactly covers cost of capital |
| $< 0$ | **Reject** — project destroys value relative to market |

# Internal Rate of Return

The IRR $r$ is the discount rate at which $NPV = 0$:

$$ C_0 = -I_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{solve for } r $$

**Linear Interpolation (Regula Falsi):** choose $i_1$ with $C_0(i_1) > 0$ and $i_2$ with $C_0(i_2) < 0$:

$$ r \approx i_1 + \frac{C_0(i_1)}{C_0(i_1) - C_0(i_2)} \cdot (i_2 - i_1) $$

| $r$ vs. $i$ | Decision |
|:-----------:|:--------:|
| $r > i$ | **Accept** |
| $r = i$ | Indifferent |
| $r < i$ | **Reject** |

> **Descartes' rule of signs:** the number of positive real roots in $q = 1+r$ equals the number of sign changes in the cash flow series, or is smaller by an even number. One sign change → exactly one IRR (above −100 %). More than one sign change → several or no IRRs are possible; use the NPV.

## Modified IRR (MIRR, Baldwin Rate)

Inflows are compounded to $t = n$ at the reinvestment rate $i$, outflows discounted to $t = 0$:

$$ MIRR = \left(\frac{TV_n}{PV_{out}}\right)^{1/n} - 1 \qquad TV_n = \sum_{CF_t > 0} CF_t \cdot (1+i)^{n-t}, \quad PV_{out} = \sum_{CF_t < 0} |CF_t| \cdot (1+i)^{-t} $$

## Incremental Investment (Differenzinvestition)

For mutually exclusive projects A and B, judge the difference B − A like a project of its own:

$$ \Delta CF_t = CF_t^{B} - CF_t^{A}, \qquad C_0^{\Delta}(i) = C_0^{B}(i) - C_0^{A}(i) $$

Choose the larger project B if $C_0^{\Delta} > 0$, i.e. if the IRR of the increment $r_{\Delta}$ exceeds $i$ (conventional increment).

# Annuity Method

The **annual value** $d$ spreads the NPV evenly across the project's useful life:

$$ d = NPV \cdot CRF(i,\,n) $$

$d$ is the equal annual surplus left after the capital service (return *of* and *on* capital at rate $i$); a positive $d$ means the project earns more than $i$ over its life — not necessarily a surplus in every single year.

> Compare projects with **different lifespans** using $d$ rather than NPV — provided both alternatives can be repeated identically (repeatability assumption). If the successor projects are known and differ, value the actual sequence instead.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Investment Appraisal with Taxes

Standard model: tax base = cash flow minus depreciation, one tax rate $s$ on project profits and on interest from the alternative investment; the result does not depend on how the project is financed.

## After-Tax Cash Flow — Volume Effect

$$ \text{Tax}_t = s \cdot (CF_{before,t} - D_t) $$

$$ CF_{after,t} = CF_{before,t} - \text{Tax}_t = CF_{before,t} \cdot (1 - s) + s \cdot D_t $$

The term $s \cdot D_t$ is the **Depreciation Tax Shield**. $I_0$ is not adjusted; it enters the tax calculation only through $D_t$.

## After-Tax Discount Rate — Interest Effect

$$ i_{after} = i \cdot (1 - s) $$

The interest of the alternative capital-market investment is taxed too, so the opportunity cost after tax falls — this is a property of the alternative, not of debt financing.

## After-Tax NPV

$$ C_0^{after} = -I_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} CF_{after,t} \cdot (1+i_{after})^{-t} $$

**Tax paradox:** $C_0^{after} > C_0^{before}$ is possible when the interest effect outweighs the volume effect — typically when tax depreciation runs ahead of economic depreciation.

## Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)

Belongs to a *different* model (different costs of debt and equity, only debt interest deductible) — do not combine it with the standard model above. For mixed equity/debt financing:

$$ r_{WACC} = k_E \cdot \frac{E}{E+D} + k_D \cdot (1-s) \cdot \frac{D}{E+D} $$

# Capital Rationing — Dean Model

## Dean Model

Investment staircase: projects sorted by IRR $r_j$ (descending). Financing staircase: sources sorted by cost $k_f$ (ascending). Where the staircases cross lies the optimal budget and the endogenous **cut-off rate** $i^*$. Assumptions: one period, independent and divisible projects.

## Profitability Index (PI)

Present value per euro of initial outlay ($PV$ = present value of all cash flows from $t = 1$, incl. $L_n$):

$$ PI = \frac{PV}{I_0} = \frac{NPV + I_0}{I_0} = 1 + \frac{NPV}{I_0} $$

For a one-period project: $PI = \dfrac{1+r}{1+i}$.

| $PI$ | Decision |
|:----:|:--------:|
| $> 1$ | **Accept** — project creates value |
| $= 1$ | Indifferent ($NPV = 0$) |
| $< 1$ | **Reject** |

Under a **binding budget constraint** $B$, rank all projects by $PI$ (descending) and fill the budget from the top. Ranking by absolute $NPV$ can crowd out efficient smaller projects (*Elephant Trap*). The PI ranking is optimal only for divisible projects and a single-period budget — with indivisible projects, check whether another combination that uses the budget more fully has a higher total NPV.

# Risk and Uncertainty

## Cash-Flow Model and Expected NPV

$$ CF_t = x \cdot (P - v) - FC $$

with volume $x$, unit price $P$ (not to be confused with the asset price $P_0$), variable cost per unit $v$ and fixed costs $FC$. With states $s$ and probabilities $p_s$ ($\sum p_s = 1$):

$$ E(CF_t) = \sum_{s} p_s \cdot CF_{t,s}, \qquad E(C_0) = -I_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{E(CF_t)}{(1+i)^t} = \sum_{s} p_s \cdot C_{0,s} $$

## Sensitivity and Break-even

For level cash flows, a change $\Delta CF$ moves the NPV by $\Delta C_0 = \Delta CF \cdot PVIFA(i,\,n)$. The break-even (critical) value of an input sets $C_0 = 0$, e.g. for the volume:

$$ x^* = \frac{I_0 / PVIFA(i,\,n) + FC}{P - v}, \qquad \text{Margin of safety} = \frac{x - x^*}{x} $$

The break-even discount rate is the IRR $r$.

## Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate

$$ i_{RA} = i + RP $$

with risk premium $RP$ for the project's risk class. Do not adjust for the same risk twice (pessimistic cash flows *and* a premium).
